claims.text: Conventionally melt-quenched phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys have relatively low thermal stability.
These alloys have a high tendency to crystallize during subsequent thermal exposure.
A brief post-quench anneal just below the crystallization onset will improve glass-forming ability.
A brief post-quench anneal just below the crystallization onset will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The effective annealing window is approximately 5–10 °C below the crystallization onset temperature.
The annealing treatment increases medium-range order in the amorphous structure.
The annealing treatment reconfigures the local atomic network of the amorphous alloy.
Controlled atomic rearrangements induced by annealing lower the free energy of the amorphous state.
Lowering the free energy of the amorphous state increases the energy barrier for crystallization.
The increased crystallization barrier stabilizes the glassy configuration.
Annealed samples will have a higher crystallization onset temperature than otherwise identical unannealed controls.
Annealed samples will exhibit delayed crystallization peaks in DSC measurements relative to unannealed controls.
The intervention should work only within a narrow annealing-temperature window just below crystallization onset.
The intervention may fail in alloys with substantially different thermal properties or crystallization kinetics.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims improved glass-forming ability, but the intervention occurs only after glass formation by melt-quenching. The predicted outcomes and experiment assess resistance to later crystallization rather than glass-forming ability itself, such as critical cooling rate or critical casting thickness.
